summary: No code, so nothing to mutate in the tree. Reviewed the two rows as TEST PRESCRIPTIONS, which is what they mostly are. M4.8b1's single hand-seeded checkpoint key cannot falsify three distinct wrong filters, and its request-count clause does not name the dimension the filter actually moves. M4.8b2 prescribes a great deal and still leaves the seq derivation, the new per-pod state, the streams/pods cost dimension, the once-active-then-quiet tick, and every runtime failure path unconstrained -- each with a concrete surviving mutation below.

findings.summary: M4.8b1's only acceptance criterion is 'A TAKEOVER TEST WITH A CHECKPOINT-SHAPED KEY PRESENT, seeded by hand'. One key, of one shape, at one position -- and by the row's own argument that position is LAST in the sort order. Three wrong filters pass it. (a) A deny-list, `!key.endsWith(".ckpt")`, instead of the allow-list the backlog.md row states ('RECOVERY MUST IGNORE NON-DELTA KEYS'): identical behaviour when the only foreign key is a .ckpt, wrong the moment M4.8c's discovery, M7's GC or a multipart temp key puts anything else under the prefix. (b) `key.contains(".delta")` instead of `endsWith`: a `ckpt/...ckpt` key contains neither string, so the seeded key cannot tell the two apart. (c) `return`/`break` instead of `continue` on a non-delta key: because the checkpoint sorts after every delta, stopping and skipping give the same answer for it -- and in `applyChain` (ChainReplay.java:313) that mutation TRUNCATES the chain and drops every offset past the foreign key, at the site the row itself calls the worse of the two. One extra seeded key kills all three: a non-delta key that sorts BETWEEN two deltas and whose name CONTAINS '.delta' -- e.g. `<seq:016x>.delta.tmp` mid-chain -- with the test asserting the offsets carried by the deltas AFTER it.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8b1 lands with `applyChain` doing `if (!stat.key().endsWith(".ckpt")) { ...decode... } else { return; }`. The prescribed takeover test is green: the checkpoint is last, so nothing is skipped and nothing is lost. At M4.8c or M7 a second key kind appears under `CommitLog.logPrefix()` -- a discovery marker, a GC tombstone, a `.tmp` from an interrupted write. Either it is decoded (deny-list) and the takeover fails exactly as today, or it sorts mid-chain (stop-instead-of-skip) and recovery silently returns offsets from a prefix of the chain, reassigning ranges already acknowledged. That is I2, produced by the very commit whose stated purpose was to make recovery ignore non-delta keys.

findings.summary: 'carrying a REQUEST-COUNT dimension and not correctness alone' does not say WHICH count, and the surrounding two sentences are all about LIST growth. A LIST-count assertion is invariant under the fix: the filter changes no LIST call at either site, so a LIST count passes with the filter, without the filter, and with the feature absent entirely -- it is a dead assertion that reads as a cost gate. The count the filter actually moves is GETs: `chainEnd` GETs the last key (ChainReplay.java:111) and `applyChain` GETs every listed key (ChainReplay.java:314). The row should say GETs, and require ZERO additional GETs per seeded non-delta key at BOTH sites.
findings.failure_scenario: The filter is implemented after the read -- `ChainEntry e; try { e = read(store, key); } catch (IOException ignored) { continue; }`, or a suffix check placed inside `read`. Correctness passes (the takeover succeeds) and the LIST count is unchanged, so both halves of the prescribed test are green. Every recovery still spends one GET per checkpoint ever written, and since nothing deletes checkpoints before M7 that is precisely the 'GET count grows WITH UPTIME on the failover path' the source row named as the defect -- reintroduced by the commit that claims to remove it, with the cost assertion present and blind.

findings.summary: 'keys across two triggers that are DISTINCT AND STRICTLY INCREASING' plus the exact-key grammar assertion does not pin `seq`. Three derivations satisfy both and are wrong. (a) `seq = checkpointCounter` (0,1,2,...) -- distinct, strictly increasing, zero-padded, grammar-conformant, body values all correct, and the key then carries no chain position at all, so M4.9's 'newest checkpoint + at most K deltas' has nothing to bound replay with and M4.8c's newest-key discovery learns only which checkpoint is newest, not where to resume. (b) An off-by-one between 'the last chain slot INCLUDED' and `nextSequence` (the next free slot) -- both distinct and strictly increasing, and at M4.9 the difference is one delta replayed twice or one skipped. The row never states the convention. (c) `new Checkpoint(0, streams, pods)` -- the body's own `sequence` field (format/Checkpoint.java:33) is not covered by 'the per-stream and per-pod values', so a constant body sequence survives every prescribed assertion while the keys increment correctly. Worse, the phrasing BIASES toward (a): if `seq` is the chain sequence and the second trigger is a T tick with no deltas in between, a CORRECT implementation produces the SAME key, so an author writing to this clause literally will pick a per-checkpoint counter. Require: key seq == body `sequence()` == a specific chain slot the workload determines, with the inclusive/exclusive convention stated.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8b2 lands with `seq` as a per-checkpoint counter and `Checkpoint.sequence` set to the same counter. Every prescribed test is green: keys distinct, strictly increasing, zero-padded, ordered pair at 9 and 16 correct, streams and pods decoded correctly, counts and boundaries exact. M4.9 then cannot bound recovery from a checkpoint at all -- it knows the newest checkpoint's ordinal and not the slot it reflects -- so either M4.9 re-derives it by replaying the chain it exists to avoid replaying, or the format changes and every writer, reader, fake and golden file changes with it (non-negotiable 8) one milestone after it was written.

findings.summary: The row correctly says per-pod `lastAppliedFlushSeq` is NEW STATE, then prescribes only 'decode what was PUT and assert the per-stream and per-pod values against a workload where they differ'. That is a round-trip, and it misses the two ways this field breaks. (a) MONOTONICITY: `pods.put(podId, flushSeq)` (last-write-wins) instead of a `Math::max` fold survives any workload whose flushSeqs only rise. The case that matters is a pod whose LATER commit carries a LOWER flushSeq -- a retry or a duplicate in flight, which is the exact case M4.10 exists for -- where a checkpoint recording the lower value re-admits a commit already applied. Note that every other fold in this code is deliberately `Math::max` for the analogous reason (ChainReplay.fold, ChainReplay.java:373). (b) PROVENANCE: nothing in the chain carries it. `CommitDelta` is `(sequence, segments)` (format/CommitDelta.java:28); `podId`/`flushSeq` exist only in `CommitRequest`, and `CommitLog`'s javadoc says the log never reads either. So the map can only be built from requests seen by the writer's own process, and the first checkpoint after a takeover or restart carries `pods = {}` -- the idempotency window emptied at the moment duplicates are most likely. A plausible variant is the mutation the surrounding code already models: gating the fold on `hop.epoch() == ownEpoch`, as `nextSequence` and `seal` are gated at ChainReplay.java:328 and :336. The row must either require an assertion on the first checkpoint written after a takeover, or state that the map is process-local and name the row that rehydrates it.
findings.failure_scenario: The writer keeps a `HashMap<String,Long>` fed by `commitAll`'s requests and `put`s into it. Both prescribed assertions pass: two pods with different flushSeqs decode exactly as written. In production, a pod retries a flush across a leader failover; the new leader's first checkpoint records either nothing for that pod (empty map) or the retry's lower flushSeq (last-write-wins), and M4.10's idempotency check then admits a commit that was already applied -- duplicate records with new offsets, invisible to every test M4.8b2 shipped.

findings.summary: 'PUTs must scale with deltas/K and seconds/T, never with streams or pods' is stated and never assigned a test. Every prescribed count assertion holds streams and pods fixed: the K boundary is 'zero PUTs after K-1 deltas, one after the Kth', the T boundary is one tick, and the multi-stream/multi-pod workload is prescribed for DECODING the body, not for counting. Surviving mutation: one checkpoint PUT per stream in the map (or per pod), e.g. a write inside the loop that builds `streams`. With a single-stream boundary workload that is one PUT, identical to correct; with the body workload nothing counts. This is the non-negotiable-6 dimension -- a request rate scaling with partitions -- so it is the one count that must not be left implicit.
findings.failure_scenario: The K boundary test uses one stream and one pod, as boundary tests naturally do. The writer emits a checkpoint object per stream. All counts are green. At 1,600 streams the checkpoint trigger issues 1,600 PUTs where the cost model says one, and the first place it is noticed is a bill or a rate limit, because the assertion that would have caught it was never written and the row's cost sentence reads as though it had been.

findings.summary: The two time-driven cases straddle a semantics the row never states, and the gap between them has a surviving mutation. 'PUTs must scale with ... seconds/T' says a tick writes every T regardless of activity; the idle clause says zero PUTs after 2T. Both can only be true if there is a changed-since-the-last-checkpoint condition, which is never named. Mutation surviving BOTH prescribed tests: the tick writes unconditionally once ANY delta has ever been committed -- a dirty flag set and never cleared. The idle test never commits, so it is zero either way; the T-liveness test commits and then samples one tick, so it is one either way. A cluster that goes quiet then PUTs forever at 1/T, and -- if `seq` is the chain sequence, per TR3 -- every one of those PUTs overwrites the SAME key, which is the 'CountingBinStore counts PUTs, not distinct keys' trap this row warns about arriving as production behaviour instead of as a mutation. Say whether a tick with nothing new since the last checkpoint writes, and assert it.
findings.failure_scenario: A cluster ingests for an hour, then goes quiet overnight. The prescribed idle test never covered this state, because it asserts idleness only from construction. The writer emits 8 hours / T checkpoints, all byte-identical, all at the same key, all invisible to the suite -- a per-second request rate that scales with wall-clock time and with nothing else, in the one component whose stated cost shape is deltas/K.

findings.summary: The only failure path prescribed is configuration validation ('K = 0 ... T = 0'). There is no RUNTIME failure path, which testing.md rule 14 requires and which this component has an obvious one of: the checkpoint PUT itself failing. Two opposite mutations both survive every prescribed test. (a) The IOException propagates to the committing caller, so an unwritable `ckpt/` key turns an optimisation into a commit outage -- and the writer sits on the commit path by construction, since the K trigger counts deltas. (b) It is swallowed with no log and no retry, so checkpointing stops permanently after one transient 503 and M4.9's bounded recovery silently degrades to the full replay it exists to remove, with nothing observable saying so. The row must choose one and assert it, with the faulty-store fake the simulation already has.
findings.failure_scenario: Under (a), a transient object-store failure on the checkpoint key fails a commit that was already durable and already sequenced, and the caller retries a segment that does not need retrying. Under (b), the store recovers but the writer does not, and the next failover replays the entire chain -- the exact unbounded recovery M4.9 is written to bound -- with every test green and no log line to explain it.

findings.summary: The source row named the fields ('per-stream `nextOffset`/`oldestRetainedOffset`, per-pod `lastAppliedFlushSeq`'); the split kept `lastAppliedFlushSeq` and dropped the other two names, leaving 'the per-stream ... values against a workload where they differ'. `oldestRetainedOffset` has no producer before M7, so no workload can make it differ and the qualifier silently excludes it. Surviving mutation: `new StreamOffsets(nextOffset, nextOffset)` -- legal, because `Checkpoint` validates only `oldest <= next` (format/Checkpoint.java:52) -- passes a test that asserts nextOffset per stream. Naming the field and saying it is 0 until M7 has a producer costs one clause and closes it.
findings.failure_scenario: The writer sets both fields from the same variable. At M7, GC reads `oldestRetainedOffset == nextOffset` for every stream and concludes nothing below the write cursor is retained, deleting segments consumers have not read. The regression was introduced two milestones earlier by a line no assertion ever constrained.

findings.summary: 'BOTH SITES' is accurate for production -- `chainEnd` (ChainReplay.java:99/111) and `applyChain` (ChainReplay.java:312/314) are the only two; `firstEntry` addresses `keyFor(0)` directly and is safe. But there is a THIRD decode site in the test fixtures, and it is the one that matters when M4.8b2 lands: `Invariants.readChain` (sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/Invariants.java:337-353) lists `logPrefix()` and hands every key to `ChainEntry.decode`, and `CommitProtocolSimulation.hasChain` (sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/CommitProtocolSimulation.java:240) treats ANY key under the prefix as proof the chain exists. Once the writer exists, the deterministic simulation (testing.md rule 20) breaks, and the tempting repair is `catch (IOException) { continue; }` -- which makes the invariant checker blind to genuine corrupt bytes and is the assertion-weakening inversion check-test-integrity.sh exists to catch, landing in the same commit as a production change. M4.8b2 should say the harness gets the same suffix ALLOW-LIST, never a swallowed decode, and that `hasChain` counts deltas rather than keys.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8b2's author runs the suite, sees CommitProtocolSimulation fail on a checkpoint object, and wraps the decode in a try/catch. Every subsequent simulation run silently skips any object it cannot decode -- including the torn and mis-versioned entries the harness injects faults to produce -- so the I1-I5 checks report CLEAN over chains they never read, and the project's strongest correctness test goes partly vacuous with no gate able to see it.

findings.summary: 'AND A FAILURE PATH FOR BOTH: `K = 0` restores a PUT per delta, `T = 0` one per tick' states a CONSEQUENCE, not a required behaviour, and the condensation dropped the source row's clause that named it 'this row's own forbidden cost shape'. Read literally it prescribes a test that PINS the forbidden cadence as expected. Negative K, a negative or null Duration, and 'K = 0 means disabled' are all unaddressed. The precedent is one class over: `BatchingSequencer` refuses `Duration.ZERO` and still admitted a sub-millisecond interval that truncated to `sleep(0)` (baselines/review.txt, rounds:M4.7). Say the constructor refuses non-positive K and T and assert the refusal.
findings.failure_scenario: A test is written as `configure(K=0); commit 5 deltas; assertEquals(5, store.puts())`. It is green, it was red before the code existed, and it now defends the cost shape the row forbids: a later change that adds a guard rejecting K=0 fails this test, and the guard is removed to make the suite pass -- production changed to satisfy the test, with a green gate.
